bibliographic.title: Copyright Law and the Lifecycle of Machine Learning Models
bibliographic.authors: Martin Kretschmer; Thomas Margoni; Pinar Oruc
bibliographic.venue: IIC (International Review of Intellectual Property and Competition Law)
bibliographic.citation_apa: Kretschmer, M., Margoni, T., & Oruc, P. (2024). Copyright law and the lifecycle of machine learning models. IIC, 55, 110–138. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40319-023-01419-3

methodology.method_family: empirical case studies with legal and policy analysis
methodology.study_design: three detailed case studies across ML application settings mapped to an industry AI lifecycle framework
methodology.sample_description: Three technological settings: (1) machine learning for scientific study of regional short-term letting markets; (2) NLP in the context of large language models; (3) computer vision for image content moderation
methodology.sector: cross-sector (scientific research, NLP/LLM industry, content moderation)
methodology.technology_context: machine learning lifecycle (collecting data, organising data, model training, model operation); foundation models; generative AI; NLP; large language models including ChatGPT and GPT-4; EU copyright and AI Act policy context

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article addresses copyright law, training-data inputs, and EU regulatory interventions (CDSM exceptions, AI Act foundation-model disclosure) across an ML lifecycle that includes an LLM/NLP case study. It does not examine conversational systems, chatbot operation, guardrails, observability, human oversight, contestation, or post-deployment monitoring of conversational AI in regulated environments. It is relevant as foundational legal-regulatory context for LLM data governance rather than central evidence on conversational governance.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: High Python relevance score driven by LLM and governance terms, but the paper's primary focus is copyright law and training-data legality rather than conversational AI governance; manual confirmation of scope fit is advised.

appraisal.notes: Appraisal based on abstract, introduction, and partial case-study excerpts only. The study combines deliberate multi-setting case studies with EU copyright legal analysis; limitations and full methods/results were not fully visible in the provided text.

cerqual.explanation: The study is coherent and methodologically appropriate for legal analysis of ML lifecycles, including LLMs, but its relevance to conversational governance in regulated operational settings is indirect and primarily limited to input-stage copyright, disclosure, and compliance policy.

coding.theme: Legal governance of machine learning model inputs across the AI lifecycle
coding.subtheme: Copyright and regulatory treatment of LLM training data in the EU

synthesis.main_claim: Copyright law centrally shapes the machine learning model lifecycle, especially at the input stage, and current EU policy moves toward copyright exceptions, opt-outs, and training-data disclosure are likely to produce a fully copyright-licensed machine learning environment with structural effects on industry, innovation, and research.
synthesis.contribution: Provides an industry lifecycle framework (collecting, organising, training, operating) and three empirical case studies—including NLP/large language models—to support legal analysis and harmonisation assessment under EU copyright law and related AI regulation.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence on legal and regulatory governance of LLM training data, copyright compliance, and EU policy instruments; not as primary evidence on conversational AI governance, operational guardrails, human oversight, or post-deployment monitoring.
